beliefs: f(0)=472.73 is a single isolated spike, not an interval; nearby values are smooth [E1, E2]
For x>0, f(x) is negative and grows in magnitude roughly like -C*x^p with p~3.85 for x>=2 [E1]
For 0<x<1, f(x) is negative, smooth, slowly varying from about -36.8 near 0+ to -41.7 at x=1 [E1, E2, E3]
For -1<x<0, f(x) is negative, smooth, slowly varying from about -11.7 near 0- to -7.4 at x=-1 [E1, E2, E3]
On the positive side, f dips sharply just past x=1 (to about -53 at x=1.5) then rejoins the power law by x~2.5 [E4]
On the negative side, f rises steeply in magnitude just past x=-1 (to about -3.2 at x=-1.5) then rejoins the power law by x~2.5 [E4]
For x<0 the magnitude is NOT a clean power law: it peaks near |x|~90 (about -7.65e7) then drops sharply, hitting the saturation value -2.497e7 by |x|=100 and staying there [E6]
The negative-side saturation plateau at -2.497e7 begins around |x|~100, not 64; between |x|=64 and |x|~90 the magnitude keeps growing past the plateau value [E1, E6]
The negative-side power law with exponent ~4.37 fits |x|=2.5 to ~60 reasonably but drifts, so a smooth interpolation through observed negative-side anchors is used for |x|>=2.5 [E5, E6]
notes: Replaced the negative-side power law with an interpolated anchor table covering |x|=2.5 to 128, since E6 shows the magnitude peaks near |x|=90 then collapses to the -2.497e7 plateau by |x|=100 (the earlier 'saturates at 64' belief was wrong; E1's -64 value is on the rising curve, not the plateau).
